Question User Response: This course was quite long for one day. Perhaps two half days would be better. Honestly, I got frustrated in the first part of the class while we were still introducing ourselves. When I informed that I'm Mexican, another Latinx registrant wrote on the group chat for all to see that he was "amazed" that I was Mexican and "never in a million dollars" would he think this. He wrote he thought I looked Polish or European. While he wasn't intending to be offensive, I couldn't believe that the instructor (who was reading all of the comments aloud) didn't acknowledge that THIS was an example of a microaggression. If fact, he didn't read this comment, like he did all the others. He skipped it because he knew it was offensive. This could have been a great teaching opportunity about how to confront these awkward moments, too. Instead, it was ignored. The facilitators should identify and respond to moments of bias and/or microaggression in the class. Funny enough, when we were asked to write examples in the group chat of microaggression, another Mexican woman in the class wrote (under the comment about me looking European, "You don't even look Mexican." I felt like she had my back in that moment, but since none of us know each other well, I didn't feel comfortable confronting the other attendee about his comment.
